pattern_stance_changes.reason: The Security-Aware condition is defined as Normal Skills plus security directives (§3.2), so the isolating contrast is Normal Skills vs Skills + Security Rules, not no-skills vs Skills + Security Rules. On that contrast AR rises from 10.1% to 14.8% and ASR falls from 25.5% to 22.3% (Table 14C). Pooled over prompt styles in Table 18a, ASR falls about 7.5 points in Prepare-Env (26.3% to 18.8%) and 5.6 points in Run-Tests (48.8% to 43.1%), and AR rises from 31.3% to 42.5% in Prepare-Env. The ASR changes are not significant. The defence wins on detection and does not lose on prevention, which is 'mixed'. The review's 22.6% vs 22.3% folds in the +2.9 points from adding the skills themselves.

The only rules contrast varies the content of security directives, which is P22 evidence. The rule files are drawn from a cross-repository pool (App. E), not the target repository's own instruction hierarchy, and no arm varies whether repository instruction files are present. Counting the same contrast under P01 double-counts it.

The 'skills hurt' evidence is task success. Table 14 gives 64.3% to 55.8%, but Table 17 gives 36.8% to 35.2% for the same Codex + GPT-5.4 runs, and Table 14's Safe-Useful (46.3%) exceeds Table 17's TSR, so the TSR numbers cannot be trusted. ASR changes by +2.9 points within overlapping CIs. The skills are randomly drawn, task-irrelevant productivity skills, and §2.1 models them as concatenated into the initial prompt, so on-demand skill loading is not what was tested.

A GPT-4o judge produces every alert-rate number in the paper (§3.4, App. H) and is validated against two human annotators (App. G.1). It is a used, relied-upon component with no comparison against an alternative oracle, which is 'introduces', not a passing mention.

missed_issues: P16 was not tagged. Run-Tests is the execution-based verifier step, and §5.1's axios case shows the agent 'continues into a fix-and-rerun loop' over the poisoned tests/setup/server.js without flagging it. The verification step most harnesses depend on is the highest-ASR invocation measured (45.5% [41.1, 50.0] with 9.4% alerts, Table 14A).

Table 1 implies payloads run without the agent ever opening the poisoned file. ASR among runs where the injected file was not read works out to about 27.5% for Run-Tests (about 44 runs) and about 50% for Prepare-Env (about 22 runs), against 26.4% when it was read. Build and test tooling (npm preinstall hooks, Gradle build scripts, test setup files) executes repository code the agent never inspected, so neither alerts nor rules text can stop these runs; only execution-level controls such as egress denial can. The paper does not report this split, and the subgroups are small.

The explanation that security rules fail because 'the alert comes too late' (§4.2(3), §7) has no timing measurement. There is no count of alerts raised before vs after the payload executed, though the traces and server logs needed for it exist.

Inference treats all 1,917 runs as independent, but they come from 20 repositories x 2 payload layouts. The Wilson CIs and HC1 errors are not clustered by repository, and there is no per-repository breakdown, so the '±3-4%' precision (§4.1) is overstated. The TIU p=0.036 is unlikely to survive clustering.

The non-Codex rows look like harness or oracle failures. Claude Code + Sonnet 4.6 has no-skills TSR 0.0% (0/610) with 53 infrastructure errors. AR is exactly 0.0% for OpenCode (0/316, 0/274) and Claude Code (0/324, 0/274) under both skill settings, with up to 160 of 484 records lost to errors (Table 17). App. G.1 does not say which agents the 192 validation traces came from. 'Claude Code is consistently the most resistant' and any per-host risk ratio are therefore not interpretable.

§7 recommends rewriting user prompts into a canonical, well-specified style, but the canonical baseline has higher ASR (25.8%) than TIU (20.5%) and SFV (21.1%) in Table 14B, so the paper's own data argue against it. Every run uses one well-known payload (cat /etc/passwd | curl -X POST), every direct-deep run uses one fixed helper path (.github/.cache/ci/workflows/hooks/telemetry/sync_helper.sh), and 373 of the 480 skills come from affaan-m/everything-claude-code, which is also one of the 20 target repositories.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats, COI none, rigor, reproducibility and relevance. I also agree with the review's claim grades, including strong for the task-type effect (5.3x, not 4.5x) and weak for the prompt-style and cross-agent claims. My generalizability is 2 rather than 3: one blatant payload at one fixed path, open egress, unconstrained automation mode, and non-Codex rows showing 0% task success or exactly 0% alerts; the merge takes 2. I move P22 from contradicts to mixed because the isolating contrast is the same skills with and without security directives, where alerts rise (10.1% to 14.8%) and attack success falls slightly and not significantly (25.5% to 22.3%). P01 and P02 move to neutral because the first double-counts that contrast and the second rests on task-success numbers that disagree between Tables 14 and 17; P18 is introduces because the GPT-4o judge produces every alert number. The review missed P16: the run-the-tests verification step is the riskiest invocation, and Table 1 implies payloads also ran when the agent never opened the poisoned file, which only execution-level controls can stop.
